rules.localIntel: Hand-curated from primary sources: each item was read at its own source on the date shown, states only what that source says, and quotes it where a quote is given. Where a source does not settle something (a winner, an end date) the item says not verified. Every link is re-checked on each daily build; an item whose source has gone is withdrawn until it is re-sourced. This is not a census: it lists the contracts, formularies and papers found and read, not every one that exists.
rules.frameworks: NO NHS SUPPLY CHAIN FRAMEWORK IS COUNTED HERE, AND THAT IS THE FINDING RATHER THAN A GAP. NHS Supply Chain's own website search returns "No results found for 'dermatology'", run 11 September 2026, and no one of the 121 framework names the Hub's record held on 11 September 2026 is this speciality's. TWO AGREEMENTS DO CARRY A DERMATOLOGY LOT AND BOTH ARE NAMED HERE RATHER THAN COUNTED. Total Patient Assessment Device Solutions, 2025/S 000-032216, 4 August 2026 to 3 August 2028, 40 suppliers, with an option to extend 24 months to 3 August 2030: NHS Supply Chain's site search for "dermatoscope" returns this agreement and no other. Its five lots are blood pressure monitors and cuffs, thermometers, patient weighing, Patient Assessment Devices and Kits, and personal health monitors; the lot a dermatoscope sits in is not stated anywhere on the public brief, because the product listing is in the Framework Matrices download, so Lot 4 is the lot whose NAME covers it and that is a reading, not a sourced statement. And Anaesthesia Machines, Ventilators, Neonatal Equipment and Phototherapy Systems, 2026/S 000-008108, 2 March 2026 to 28 February 2029, 25 suppliers, whose Lot 4 the brief names verbatim as "Adult and Paediatric Phototherapy Devices" - adult phototherapy being narrowband UVB and PUVA, which is this patch, while Lot 3 neonatal equipment is the maternity and neonatal page's. WHY NEITHER IS COUNTED: NHS Supply Chain publishes supplier names per agreement and never per lot, so claiming either would publish its whole list as this speciality's market - weighing scales, thermometers and ECG from the first, ventilators and incubators from the second. Both references are given above so a rep can go straight to the right agreement. Every date, reference and count in this paragraph was read on NHS Supply Chain's own brief on 11 September 2026. COVERAGE LIMITS, STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. THIS IS A PATCH WITH NO FRAMEWORK AND THEREFORE NO FRAMEWORK SUPPLIER LIST, AND THE EMPTY FRAMEWORKS SECTION AND EMPTY FRAMEWORK-NAMED SUPPLIER LIST ARE THE ANSWER, NOT A FAILURE TO LOAD. The suppliers shown are directory-tagged, and are labelled so. NHS Supply Chain's own site search returns no results at all for 'dermatology', run 11 September 2026, and its Procurement Calendar carries no dermatology row. The two agreements that do carry a dermatology lot are named in full in the frameworks rule, with their references, dates and lot names, so a rep can go to the right agreement without this panel publishing sixty-five suppliers of thermometers, weighing scales and ventilators as a dermatology market. MOST OF THE AWARDS BELOW ARE SERVICE CONTRACTS, NOT PRODUCT CONTRACTS, AND THAT IS WHAT THIS MARKET LOOKS LIKE. Fifteen of the twenty matched notices name a dermatology service in their title: Integrated Care Board and trust commissioning of community dermatology, teledermatology, outsourced clinics, medical photography and urgent skin cancer triage. A product supplier's route into those is the provider who won them, not the notice. When every award on this panel was read on 29 September 2026, the only dermatology product purchase among them was Calderdale and Huddersfield's dermatoscopes and image transfer system, published in 2021. TWO AWARDS ARE A THREE-SPECIALITY MEDICINES BASKET and are included because skin is named in the title, not because the whole award is this patch: NHS National Services Scotland's 'ENT, Ophthalmology & Skin Medicines/Medical Devices', 2022 and 2024. Read them as a route in, not as a dermatology contract value. THE DRUG TARIFF SLICE IS THE EMOLLIENT RANGE, AS NHSBSA ITSELF CLASSIFIES IT. It is every Part IXA line NHSBSA files under BNF 21.22: the emollient creams, ointments, gels, washes and bath additives, the menthol-in-aqueous and other antipruritic creams, and the heel, callus and diabetic foot creams filed with them. It is the honest supplier list for this patch, but it is not the whole dermatology prescribing bill: topical corticosteroids, topical retinoids, antifungals, isotretinoin and every biologic NICE has appraised for atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, prurigo nodularis and hidradenitis suppurativa are Part VIII medicines, not Part IX appliances; the generic medicines among them are in the Part VIIIA slice shown separately, and branded medicines are in no part of the Drug Tariff this panel holds. THESE LINES ALSO SIT INSIDE THE PART IXA TOTAL THE TISSUE VIABILITY AND WOUND CARE PAGE CARRIES WHOLE, which is stated so nobody reads the two panels as counting different things. WHAT IS NOT HERE: wigs, which most often serve chemotherapy alopecia and which NHS Supply Chain buys under an agreement this page states is not a dermatology agreement; systemic melanoma and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma therapy, which is the oncology patch; skin graft, skin substitute and cryopreserved allograft, which are plastics, burns and reconstruction's; peristomal barrier creams, which are Part IXC and the stoma pages'; antiseptic skin cleansing and disinfection, which is infection prevention's (the emollient washes and soap substitutes NHSBSA files under 21.22, such as QV Gentle wash and Aquamax wash, are counted here); and the AI skin lesion triage NICE names in HTG746, which is a per-referral licence bought by an individual teledermatology service and has no framework at all, so no panel can carry it.

rules.awards: Award-stage notices whose TITLE matches /\b((?:tele)?dermatolog\w*|dermatoscop\w*|dermoscop\w*|skin cancer|skin lesion\w*|skin medicines|melanoma|basal cell carcinoma|cutaneous squamous cell|mohs|psoria\w*|eczema|atopic dermatitis|dermatitis|acne|rosacea|urticaria|hidradenitis|vitiligo|prurigo|pruritus|pemphig\w*|epidermolysis bullosa|ichthyos\w*|alopecia|actinic keratos\w*|emollient\w*|isotretinoin|narrowband uvb|narrow[- ]band uvb|puva)\b/i. NO EXCLUSION LIST IS APPLIED, because every notice this pattern matched was read one by one and all of them are this speciality. The loose terms that would have needed excluding were refused from the pattern above instead of admitted and then argued with. A CPV code beginning 85121282 is recorded as corroboration where the feed carries one, but never admits a notice on its own: a notice carrying a basket of CPV codes is filed under all of them and bought under one. Buyer names are never matched on.
rules.openTenders: Notices still open for bidding, matched the same way. An empty list means no open notice on this patch today, not that none was looked for.
rules.drugTariff: NHSBSA Drug Tariff Part IXA for the stated effective month, narrowed to the lines NHSBSA itself files under BNF 21.22, and then summarised. The BNF code is NHSBSA's own classification of each line and is used in preference to matching the product name, because a name cannot see a branded product: NHSBSA lists many brands as "Generic <brand name>", which says nothing about what the product is. A line published without a BNF code is counted only if its virtual medicinal product description matches /emollient|emulsifying wax|(?:white|yellow) soft paraffin|liquid paraffin|paraffin-free|\burea \d|lauromacrogols|eczema|dry skin balm|heel balm|hand balm|skin balm|callus removing/i. The part is sliced rather than claimed whole because the part is not this speciality: Part IXA is 56,833 lines, most of them dressings and elastic hosiery, which are the tissue viability page's. Every count and price below is taken from the lines selected. Prices are the reimbursement price at publication, converted from the pence NHSBSA publishes, and are not necessarily today's.
rules.directorySuppliers: Companies the Hub's own supplier directory files under this speciality, from the speciality labels on each company's directory record, resolved through speciality-label-map.json and speciality-map.json (Compare ids: dermatology). They are labelled DIRECTORY-TAGGED because the tag is the Hub's filing of a company's range, not a procurement record: being listed here is not evidence of a contract or of volume, and the list is not a census of the market. A company that is also on this speciality's own frameworks is listed once, with the framework-named suppliers, and marked as also directory-tagged. WHERE A COMPANY IS ON ANOTHER FRAMEWORK: where a directory-tagged company is named on an NHS Supply Chain framework that is not counted as this speciality's, it is still listed, with that framework named against it and linked, so it is not lost from the page. 8 of the 17 listed here carry such a note. Framework names and links come from NHS Supply Chain's own contract launch briefs as held in frameworks.json; an agreement the directory records from another buying organisation, such as an NHS Shared Business Services framework, is shown as the directory states it.
rules.gpPrescribing: Items prescribed in primary care in England (GP practices and other prescribers NHSBSA attributes to a practice) and dispensed in the community, aggregated to ICB. Not hospital in-patient use, and not the trust-level hospital prescribing dataset. Source: NHSBSA Open Data: English Prescribing Dataset (EPD) with SNOMED code. Each market below is a set of BNF codes exactly as NHSBSA classifies them, named with the market. Figures are for the latest month in the dataset (202607) with a 12-month total; a change on the same month a year earlier is published only where that month had at least 25 items, and otherwise no percentage is printed. Share is share of ITEMS by NHSBSA product (BNF code characters 1 to 11, split to 13 where a catch-all code holds several brands). It is product share, not company share: the dataset does not name the company, and one company can hold several products. An ICB's leaders are ranked within that ICB's own total for the same market and month. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0. Source: NHS Business Services Authority.
rules.mhraDsu: Every MHRA Drug Safety Update that GOV.UK itself tags to a therapeutic area mapped to this speciality in config/mhra-dsu-speciality-map.json. The speciality comes only from GOV.UK's own facet, never from the title or the text. The monthly 'Letters and medicine recalls sent to healthcare professionals' roundup is left out (5 here). Newest first; the count is every tagged update in the archive, and the list shows the most recent. MHRA Drug Safety Update, GOV.UK, as at 2026-09-30.
rules.drugTariffViiia: NHSBSA Drug Tariff Part VIIIA, the basic prices of generic medicines, for effective month 2026-09: narrowed to the lines whose medicine NHSBSA prescribes under BNF chapter 13. The BNF code is the one NHSBSA attaches to the line's VMP SNOMED code in its English Prescribing Dataset, the same classification-first approach as the Part IX slice, never a medicine-name pattern. 53 of the 3,533 lines in the file carry no BNF code because the medicine was not prescribed in primary care in the months read, so this slice can understate the range and does not overstate it. Every count and price is taken from the lines selected. Prices are the basic price at publication, converted from the pence NHSBSA publishes, and are not necessarily today's. The list shows at most 80 lines, Category M first.
rules.marketShare: Computed at every build from NHSBSA data, not bought in and not estimated. PRIMARY CARE: every item dispensed in England against a GP practice prescription, English Prescribing Dataset with SNOMED code, for the BNF codes named on each market (13.02.01, 21.22), latest month 202607, with a 12-month total. SECONDARY CARE: NHS trust prescriptions dispensed in a community pharmacy (NHSBSA hospital prescribing dispensed in the community), the same BNF codes, 12 months; it is not in-hospital use, which NHSBSA publishes only by chemical substance and so cannot show a brand. DRUG TARIFF: every Part IX line NHSBSA files under the same BNF codes, in any part, counted in tariff lines per supplier, which measures what is listed and reimbursable, not what is sold. A BRAND is the first word of NHSBSA's product label, so the products of one range are counted together; a label that names its supplier in brackets stays on its own, and every generic is one row. Share is share of ITEMS, never company share: the data does not name the company, and one company can own several brands. A change on a year earlier is printed only where that month had at least 25 items. An ICB's share is the brand's items as a share of that ICB's whole market in the same month.

localIntel.title: RD005 Emollient preferred product list
localIntel.fact: A preferred list of products to be used first line: Cetraben lotion; Epimax Original, Epimax ExCetra, Aquamax, QV and Cetraben creams; Epimax, Hydromol and Cetraben ointments; Dermol cream and Dermol 500 lotion; ImuDERM. Epimax Oatmeal is marked second line, if other emollients are not tolerated. Where a specialist advises a bath or shower product, the first-line products are Hydromol Bath & Shower, QV Gentle Wash or Aquamax Wash. QV Cream is listed at £5.96 per 500g (Drug Tariff March 2021 prices).
localIntel.quote: the recommended first-line products would be Hydromol® Bath & Shower, QV® Gentle Wash or Aquamax® Wash
localIntel.use: QV Cream and QV Gentle Wash are both on the first-line list here. The document prints named company contacts: use the link, never copy those details.

localIntel.org: Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Berkshire West ICB
localIntel.title: BOB ICB Emollient Guideline, version 1.0
localIntel.fact: No first-line or second-line tiers; products are grouped by light, medium and heavy emollient, with an asterisk on the most cost-effective options (Epimax Original, Isomol, ExCetra and ointment, 50:50 and emulsifying ointment, Hydromol Intensive, Dermol 500). QV Skin Lotion is listed under light emollients, without the asterisk. Zerodouble gel is marked 2nd line and Cetraben ointment not 1st line. Cetraben cream, Diprobase Advanced Eczema cream and Epaderm ointment are Green Restricted due to cost; Oilatum cream and Doublebase gel have Block status. The guideline replaced the three previous place-based guidelines.
localIntel.quote: QV Skin Lotion (white soft paraffin 5%) 500ml pump
localIntel.use: QV is on the list but not marked cost-effective. Review due January 2027: the window to make a case is before then.

localIntel.title: Sheffield skin formulary choices: Abbreviated guide to emollients used in primary care
localIntel.date: Approved by Formulary Subgroup and Area Prescribing Group January 2023
localIntel.fact: Ranked by product type. Creams: 1st Epimax Original, 2nd Epimax ExCetra, 3rd ZeroAQS. Ointments: 1st Fifty:50, 2nd AproDerm, 3rd Zeroderm. Gels: 1st Epimax Isomol, 2nd AproDerm gel, 3rd MyriBase. Lotions: 1st QV skin lotion, 2nd Cetraben lotion. Colloidal oat: 1st Epimax oatmeal cream, 2nd Miclaro, 3rd AproDerm. QV Intensive Ointment is listed among the ointment alternatives. The printed review date, January 2026, has passed.
localIntel.use: QV skin lotion is the first-line lotion here. The review date has passed, so the next version could move it either way.

localIntel.title: BNSSG Formulary Emollient Products for Adults and Children, version 2.2
localIntel.fact: Green is first line, Blue second line. Green: 50:50 WSP in LP, Epimax ointment, AproDerm ointment, Epimax Original and ExCetra creams, Epimax Isomol gel, Cetraben lotion, Epimax oatmeal cream, Dermol 500 lotion, Menthoderm, ImuDERM. Blue includes Zeroderm ointment, Epimax paraffin-free ointment, Exocream, AproDerm cream and gel, Adex gel, Doublebase Once gel, E45 lotion, Miclaro, Emollin, Balneum Plus and Hydromol Intensive. QV does not appear. The version history records the number of emollients per category being reduced in 2025.
localIntel.quote: Green – First line. Any AHP to prescribe.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the current list. The previous version (9.3, below) did list QV Skin lotion.

localIntel.title: Barnsley emollient formulary choices guidance
localIntel.date: Ratified by Barnsley APC 11/10/2023; minor updates October 2024 and September 2025
localIntel.fact: Ointments: 1st line Fifty:50, 2nd line AproDerm ointment. Gels: 1st Epimax Isomol, 2nd AproDerm gel. Lotions: 1st line Miclaro oat lotion, 2nd line QV skin lotion. localIntel.quote: Light emollients Formulary First choices Zero AQS cream QV lotion
localIntel.use: QV lotion is a first choice light emollient on the GM formulary.

localIntel.title: Humber and North Yorkshire Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: Tiers differ by area. Humber first choice includes Zerocream, Epimax cream, AproDerm Colloidal Oat, Zerobase, Zerodouble, Zeroguent, Zeroderm, Fifty:50, ZeroAQS and Dermol 500; Humber second choice includes QV cream, QV ointment, Cetraben lotion, Epaderm and Hydromol ointment. North Yorkshire and York first line: Zerocream, Epimax cream, Aquamax cream, emulsifying ointment, Flexitol urea. There QV cream is a third-line choice and QV ointment is non-formulary.
localIntel.quote: Humber: Second Choice Only for prescribing when 1st-line emollients have not been effective
localIntel.use: QV is second choice in Humber and third line or non-formulary in North Yorkshire and York.

localIntel.org: North East and North Cumbria ICB
localIntel.title: NENC Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No tiers on the web page: every product listed is marked Formulary, including the AproDerm and Epimax ranges, Aquamax, Cetraben, Emollin, Hydromol, 50:50, the Zero range, QV cream and QV Intensive ointment. The linked NENC Emollient Prescribing Guideline (approved October 2024) is behind a captcha and its tiers were not read.
localIntel.use: QV cream and QV Intensive are on the NENC formulary; whether the guideline ranks them is not verified.

localIntel.title: Cheshire and Merseyside Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.date: Review date not filled in on the page
localIntel.fact: No tiers stated: a long formulary list grouped by type, including Cetraben, E45, Diprobase, Zeroguent, the Epimax range, Zerobase, Doublebase, Hydromol, Epaderm and Aveeno. QV 5% lotion and QV cream are listed. QV oil and QV gentle wash sit among the bath and wash products NHS England says should not be routinely prescribed.
localIntel.use: QV lotion and cream are listed without a tier.

localIntel.title: Lancashire and South Cumbria Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No tiers stated. Named products include emulsifying ointment, the Epimax range, Hydromol ointment, 50:50, Oilatum cream, ZeroAQS, Dermol, Balneum Plus (restricted), Hydromol Intensive and ImuDERM. QV does not appear.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the LSC formulary.

localIntel.org: West Yorkshire ICB: Calderdale, Kirklees and Wakefield
localIntel.title: Emollient Prescribing Guidelines, v2.0
localIntel.ends: Due to be reviewed February 2026, passed
localIntel.fact: Locally agreed choices, no first-line or second-line tiers. Creams: Epimax Original, Epimax ExCetra, AproDerm, Cetraben. Ointments: Epimax, Zeroderm, Hydromol. Also Epimax paraffin-free, Oatmeal and Isomol, ImuDERM, Balneum Intensiv and Dermol. QV does not appear.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the list, and the guideline is past its review date.

localIntel.title: Leeds Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: Ranked choices: first choice Epimax ointment, Fifty:50, Epimax Original and ImuDERM; second choice Zerocream; then emulsifying ointment and Zerodouble; Zerobase and Zeroderm; Hydromol and Oilatum; Epaderm and Doublebase. QV Intensive ointment is listed as Formulary but not stocked at Leeds Teaching Hospitals.
localIntel.use: QV Intensive is on the Leeds formulary but not in the ranked choices.

localIntel.title: Nottinghamshire Emollient Formulary V5.1
localIntel.fact: First line is shown green and second line blue, by cell colour, which text extraction does not keep; the tiers were not read here. QV does not appear anywhere in the document.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the Nottinghamshire formulary.

localIntel.title: Lincolnshire Emollient formulary
localIntel.date: December 2022, reviewed by ULHT dermatology and Lincolnshire ICB
localIntel.fact: First line options include Epimax ointment, Fifty:50, Zeroderm and Emollin (severe); Epimax Isomol, Zerodouble, Epimax Original and ExCetra (moderate); Epimax Original and Epimax oatmeal (mild). Second line options include Cetraben ointment, Hydromol, AproDerm gel, Doublebase, Zerobase, Cetraben cream, Zerocream, Cetraben lotion, Zeroveen and AproDerm oat. QV does not appear.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the Lincolnshire formulary.

localIntel.title: LLR Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: Preferred emollients and soap substitutes: Epimax cream, ZeroAQS, Aquamax, Isomol gel, Zerodouble, AproDerm cream, Zerobase, Oilatum cream, emulsifying ointment, 50:50, Zeroderm and Hydromol ointment. The linked Leicestershire Emollient Formulary PDF dates from 2016. QV does not appear.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the LLR formulary.

localIntel.title: BSol Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No tiers stated. Formulary products include the AproDerm and Epimax ranges, emulsifying ointment, Hydromol, Hydrous ointment, 50:50, white soft paraffin and the Zero range; Epaderm only where other options are unsuitable. QV and QV bath additive are Non Formulary.
localIntel.use: QV is non-formulary in Birmingham and Solihull.

localIntel.title: Black Country Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No tiers stated. Formulary products include Cetraben cream, Epimax Original and ExCetra, the Zero range, Dermol 500, Aquadrate, Dermatonics and E45 Itch Relief. QV does not appear.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the Black Country formulary.

localIntel.title: HW Emollient Prescribing Guidelines v2.2.1
localIntel.date: Updated August 2026 (MPC approved extension); original approved August 2020
localIntel.fact: Preferred products ranked most cost-effective first. Ointments: Fifty:50, emulsifying ointment, Epimax, Zeroderm, Epimax paraffin-free, Hydromol, Cetraben, QV Intensive. Creams: Epimax Original, ExCetra and Oatmeal, ZeroAQS, AproDerm, Zerobase, Oilatum, QV cream, Ultrabase. Gels: Epimax Isomol, AproDerm, Zerodouble, Doublebase Dayleve. Lotions: QV skin lotion, then Cetraben lotion. The H&W web formulary marks QV Lotion as the first choice emollient lotion.
localIntel.use: QV skin lotion is the top-ranked lotion; QV cream and QV Intensive are near the bottom of their lists.

localIntel.title: Shropshire and Telford Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: First choice includes Epimax ExCetra, Original and Moisturising, AproDerm cream, gel and ointment, Epimax Isomol, E45 lotion, Epimax Oatmeal and AproDerm Colloidal Oat. Second choice: Zerocream, Zerodouble, Zeroderm and Zeroveen. QV skin lotion is listed as Formulary, only if a lanolin-free lotion is needed.
localIntel.quote: QV skin lotion (ONLY FOR USE IF lanolin free lotion is needed.)
localIntel.use: QV skin lotion is on the formulary with a restriction.

localIntel.title: Emollient Formulary Choices, version 1
localIntel.date: Approved by IMOG September 2025, ratified November 2025
localIntel.fact: First line (cost-effective options) includes Aquaderm 50:50, 50:50, Aquaderm hydrous ointment, emulsifying ointment, Zeroderm, Epimax Isomol, MyriBase gel and cream, Epimax Original, ZeroAQS, Aquamax, Exocream and Zerocream. Second line, when first line is not suitable or tolerated: Emollin, Hydromol ointment, Cetraben ointment and cream, Zeroguent, Epimax paraffin-free, Zerodouble, Zerobase, QV cream and E45 cream.
localIntel.quote: Second line : to be used when 1st line is not suitable/tolerated
localIntel.use: QV cream is second line on a list ratified in November 2025.

localIntel.org: Bedfordshire, Luton and Milton Keynes (Bedfordshire and Luton formulary)
localIntel.title: Bedfordshire and Luton Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: First choice: Epimax creams, Zerobase, Zerocream, Epimax ointment and Zeroderm. The QV emollient range and QV Gentle Wash are Non Formulary. The Milton Keynes formulary also lists QV emollients as Non Formulary.
localIntel.use: QV is non-formulary across BLMK.

localIntel.title: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Formulary: 13.02 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No first-line tiers for primary care: most emollients are marked as self-care in primary care. QV (lotion, cream) and QV bath additive are Non Formulary. The linked C&P ICB emollient guideline now redirects to another site and was not read.
localIntel.use: QV is non-formulary.

localIntel.title: HWE ICS Emollient Guidelines in Adults, V1.0
localIntel.fact: Creams 1st choice: Epimax Original cream or Epimax Isomol gel. 2nd choice: Zerocream, Epimax ExCetra or Doublebase gel. Ointments that may be 1st choice: 50/50, emulsifying ointment, Epimax paraffin-free. QV does not appear in the guideline.
localIntel.use: QV is not in the guideline.

localIntel.title: Mid and South Essex Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.date: Entries in line with the MSEMOC December 2023 formulary review
localIntel.fact: No tiers stated. Formulary products include AproDerm, AquaDerm, the Epimax range, ZeroAQS, Zeroderm, Hydromol ointment, ImuDERM, Dermol and Emollin. QV cream, QV 5% skin lotion, QV gentle wash and QV bath additive are Non Formulary following the December 2023 review.
localIntel.quote: In line with Emollient formulary review (MSEMOC December 2023)
localIntel.use: QV was made non-formulary in the December 2023 review.

localIntel.title: Norfolk and Waveney Primary Care Emollient Pathway, version 1.4
localIntel.fact: First line simple emollient creams: Epimax cream, Exocream, Zerobase. First line ointments: Epimax ointment, EmulsiFess, Fifty:50. Second line humectant emollients, for patients in whom simple first-line emollients are not effective (and first line for psoriasis and hyperkeratotic skin): Epimax Isomol gel, Epimax ExCetra and QV cream.
localIntel.quote: First line for patients with psoriasis and other dry hyperkeratotic skin conditions.
localIntel.use: QV cream is second line, and first line for psoriasis and hyperkeratotic skin.

localIntel.org: Suffolk and North East Essex (Ipswich and East Suffolk formulary)
localIntel.title: Ipswich and East Suffolk Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: First choice: Epimax Original, Isomol, Oatmeal and ointment. Second choice: Zeroderm, Zerobase, Zerodouble, Zeroveen. Third choice: Hydromol ointment; Cetraben cream is a restricted third-line option. QV and QV bath additive are Non Formulary. The SNEE emollient guidance PDF sits behind a login and was not read.
localIntel.use: QV is non-formulary.

localIntel.title: NCL Joint Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No ICB-wide tiers on the page; notes are per trust, one stating Epimax ExCetra is the preferred choice per the NCL emollient guideline (not linked). QV topical, QV bath oil and QV wash are Non Formulary.
localIntel.use: QV is non-formulary.

localIntel.title: South East London Emollient Guidance for Adults and Children
localIntel.fact: No tiers: preferred product tables. Ointments: AproDerm, emulsifying, Epimax, Hydromol, 50/50, Zeroderm. Creams: AproDerm, Aquamax, Epimax, Epimax Oatmeal and ExCetra, ZeroAQS, Zerobase, Zerocream. Gels: Epimax Isomol, AproDerm, Zerodouble. Lotions: E45 and QV lotion, marked as possibly suitable for OTC purchase. QV Gentle Wash is an option on the specialist letter for exceptional bath or shower use.
localIntel.quote: QV® Lotion 500ml = £5.32 WSP 5% May be suitable for OTC purchase
localIntel.use: QV lotion is a preferred lotion. The guidance is past its review date.

localIntel.title: SWL Joint Medicines Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No tiers stated. Formulary products include Aquamax, Balneum Plus, Cetraben (noting Epimax ExCetra is more cost-effective in primary care), Epimax Original and Isomol, Zerobase, Zerocream, Zeroguent, emulsifying ointment, Epaderm, Hydromol, Fifty:50, Zeroderm and Dermol 500. QV does not appear.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the SWL formulary.

localIntel.title: Emollient Prescribing Guidance for Adults and Children
localIntel.fact: Three columns: most, medium and least cost-effective, with *** marking preferred. Preferred: Epimax Original cream, Epimax Isomol gel, Epimax ointment, Epimax Oatmeal cream. Other most cost-effective: Epimax ExCetra, ExmaQS, Aquamax, EmulsifEss, Fifty:50. QV Cream and QV Lotion are in the least cost-effective column.
localIntel.use: QV sits in the least cost-effective column. The guidance is past its review date.

localIntel.title: Sussex Formulary: 13.1 Dry and scaling skin disorders
localIntel.fact: No product carries a line flag. Notes name ZeroAQS as the 2nd line preferred option to aqueous cream, Zerobase as preferred alternative to Diprobase and Zerodouble to Doublebase. QV cream and QV Intensive ointment are listed with a note that they contain sensitisers.
localIntel.use: QV cream and Intensive are listed, flagged for parabens.

localIntel.title: Surrey Heartlands APC Emollient Prescribing Guidelines (September 2025 update)
localIntel.date: Agreed by Surrey Heartlands APC September 2025
localIntel.fact: Three bands: most, medium and least cost-effective. Most cost-effective includes Epimax Isomol, Original, ExCetra, ointment and oatmeal, ExmaQS, Aquamax, EmulsifEss, Fifty:50 and ImuDERM. QV cream and QV lotion are in the least cost-effective band.
localIntel.use: QV is in the least cost-effective band of a guideline updated in 2025.

localIntel.title: Frimley Joint Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No tiers stated; the page directs primary care to equivalent Epimax, Zero range and AproDerm products. QV emollient, proprietary QV preparations and QV bath additive are all Non Formulary.
localIntel.use: QV is non-formulary.

localIntel.org: Hampshire and Isle of Wight ICB
localIntel.title: HIOW Joint Medicines Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: No formal tiers; notes point to Epimax or Zeroderm ointments as first line, Epimax ExCetra and Epimax Oatmeal as the cost-effective choices. QV cream and QV Intensive are Non Formulary: following evidence and cost evaluation, QV products are not supported for routine prescribing locally. QV Gentle Wash is Non Formulary, self care.
localIntel.quote: QV products are not supported for routine prescribing locally.
localIntel.use: An explicit local decision against QV: the objection a QV rep has to answer here.

localIntel.title: Dorset Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.date: No date printed; linked first-line emollient PDF V2, March 2021
localIntel.fact: First choice: AproDerm Colloidal Oat, Epimax Isomol gel, Oilatum cream, Epimax cream, 50:50 ointment, Zeroderm. QV and QV bath additive are Non Formulary.
localIntel.use: QV is non-formulary.

localIntel.org: Bath and North East Somerset, Swindon and Wiltshire ICB
localIntel.title: BSW Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.date: Emollient table approved by BSW APC October 2023, updated August 2024
localIntel.fact: The BSW web formulary lists QV skin lotion as second line, only if a lanolin-free lotion is needed; QV Cream and QV Gentle Wash are for Great Western Hospital in-patients only, not for use in primary care. The BSW emollient table (adapted from BNSSG) shows green first line and blue second line.
localIntel.quote: Second line ONLY FOR USE if lanolin free lotion is needed
localIntel.use: QV skin lotion is second line; QV cream is hospital in-patient only.

localIntel.title: Dermatology Emollient Quick Reference Guide
localIntel.fact: Two columns: cost-effective brands (the Epimax range, Aquamax, ZeroAQS, AproDerm, Exocream, Zerocream, Miclaro, MyriBase, Fifty:50, Zeroderm, Dermipar, E45 lotion) and similar less cost-effective brands. QV Cream, QV Intensive and QV skin lotion are in the less cost-effective column.
localIntel.use: QV is listed as a less cost-effective brand.

localIntel.title: Devon Formulary: 13.2.1 Emollients
localIntel.fact: Products are shown as first or second line by page styling, which was not read as text here. QV does not appear on the page.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the Devon formulary.

localIntel.org: Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly ICB
localIntel.title: Emollient prescribing guidelines (V10.3)
localIntel.date: Updated June 2024; minor formatting revision April 2026
localIntel.fact: Epimax cream or Zerobase cream is first line for creams, Epimax ointment or Zeroderm ointment for ointments. QV does not appear.
localIntel.use: QV is not in the Cornwall guidelines.

localIntel.title: Emollient Formulary (Gloucestershire)
localIntel.fact: No tiers: light (Epimax Original, ZeroAQS), medium (Epimax Isomol, Zerodouble, Epimax ExCetra, Zerobase) and heavy (50:50, AproDerm ointment, Zeroderm), with a cost-effective switch table. QV appears only as QV Gentle Wash, which patients may purchase but which is not recommended for NHS prescribing.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the prescribing list.

localIntel.org: NHS Lothian, Borders and Fife (East Region Formulary)
localIntel.title: East Region Formulary: Eczema
localIntel.date: Content agreed 15/12/2021; QV 5% skin lotion removed 30/05/2024
localIntel.fact: Light emollients: first choice Zerobase 11% cream; second choice Oilatum cream, Cetraben cream, QV cream, Zerodouble gel, Zeroveen. Heavy: first choice Hydromol ointment; second choice 50:50 and emulsifying ointment. QV Gentle wash is a third choice soap substitute. QV 5% skin lotion was removed because it was no longer on the Drug Tariff.
localIntel.quote: Removal of 'QV 5% skin lotion' as no longer on drug tariff.
localIntel.use: QV cream is a second choice in south-east Scotland.

localIntel.org: West of Scotland (includes NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde)
localIntel.title: West of Scotland Formulary: Eczema
localIntel.fact: Medium-weight creams listed in cost order, no tiers: Epimax original, Zerobase, Cetraben, QV cream; Epimax isomol, Zerodouble; Epimax oatmeal, Zeroveen. Heavy: first choice 50:50 and Zeroderm, second Hydromol, third Epimax paraffin-free. QV Gentle wash is second choice for washing, on specialist recommendation.
localIntel.use: QV cream is listed last in cost order; QV Gentle wash is a second choice wash.

localIntel.title: Grampian Area Formulary: 13.02.01 Emollients
localIntel.fact: First choice: ImuDERM, Epimax Isomol gel, QV Lotion and Hydromol bath and shower. QV Cream and QV Gentle Wash are Formulary. Epimax Original and Epimax ointment are Non Formulary, noting local preference for alternatives.
localIntel.use: QV Lotion is a first choice in Grampian.

localIntel.title: Northern Ireland Formulary: 13.2.1 Emollients
localIntel.fact: Ointment formulary choices: Zeroderm, Hydromol or Cetraben. Creams: Epimax original, ExCetra and oatmeal as cost-effective options, Cetraben cream if those are not suitable. Other: 1st choice MyriBase gel, 2nd choice Emollin spray. QV does not appear.
localIntel.use: QV is not on the Northern Ireland Formulary.

localIntel.title: PTHB Emollient Prescribing Guidelines for Adults and Children
localIntel.date: Approved by Area Prescribing Group July 2025
localIntel.fact: Refers to the separate PTHB Emollient Formulary for approved products. QV does not appear in this guideline.
localIntel.use: QV is not in the Powys guideline.

updates.title: Botulinum toxin type A products: updated warnings regarding risk of iatrogenic botulism
updates.summary: Cases of iatrogenic botulism have been reported following the therapeutic or cosmetic use of botulinum toxin containing products where the toxin’s effect extends beyond the area of treatment. Patients should seek immediate medical advice if they experience signs and symptoms.

updates.title: Finasteride and Dutasteride – updated safety warnings for psychiatric side effects and sexual dysfunction
updates.summary: The MHRA has reviewed the evidence for finasteride and dutasteride and the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours and has recommended further measures to minimise this risk.

updates.title: Isotretinoin – changes to prescribing guidance and additional risk minimisation measures
updates.summary: The Commission on Human Medicines (CHM) has endorsed changes to the risk minimisation measures for isotretinoin, following a review of the impact of the measures implemented in 2023. We ask healthcare professionals to review these new measures and supporting materials and integrate them into their clinical practice.

updates.title: Isotretinoin – updates to prescribing guidance and survey of services
updates.summary: The Commission on Human Medicines (CHM) has endorsed changes to isotretinoin prescribing guidance. In addition, CHM is seeking further information from dermatology services who prescribe isotretinoin to inform any future changes to current risk minimisation measures.

updates.title: #MedSafetyWeek (3-9 November 2025): A call to action to improve patient safety
updates.summary: The annual #MedSafetyWeek campaign takes place from 3 to 9 November 2025. This year’s campaign theme is ‘we can all help make medicines safer.’

updates.title: Paracetamol and pregnancy - reminder that taking paracetamol during pregnancy remains safe
updates.summary: Patients should be reminded and reassured that there is no evidence that taking paracetamol during pregnancy causes autism in children. Paracetamol is recommended as the first-choice pain reliever for pregnant women, used at the lowest dose and for the shortest duration. It also acts as an antipyretic and is therefore used to treat fever.

updates.title: Thiopurines and intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
updates.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) has been rarely reported in patients treated with azathioprine products and is believed to be a risk applicable to all drugs in the thiopurine class (azathioprine, mercaptopurine and tioguanine). Cholestasis of pregnancy associated with thiopurines tends to occur earlier in pregnancy than non drug-induced cholestasis of pregnancy, and elevated bile acid levels may not reduce with ursodeoxycholic acid.

updates.title: Yellow Card Biobank: call to contribute to study of genetic links to side effects
updates.summary: Support this initiative to explore whether there is a genetic basis of side effects associated with direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) and allopurinol.
